title: Meta ships Muse Wonder, its first frontier-class model, with persistent memory
subtitle: The Superintelligence Lab's two new models land at Opus-tier pricing but score below Claude Opus 5.5 on the independent Artificial Analysis index — Meta is betting that memory and agent focus matter more than raw benchmarks.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Meta released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full on Monday, October 12, 2026, calling them its first frontier-class models. Wonder is sold through the Meta Model API at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens — the same price as Claude Opus 5.5. Wonder Full is restricted to Muse Code subscribers at $50 per month for the Power tier and $200 per month for the Maximum tier, with no API access. Both support a 1-million-token context window and accept text, image, video, and audio input, with text-only output. Training ran on Meta's one-gigawatt Prometheus data center in Ohio.

The pitch is less about raw capability than about state. Meta is leading with two new features — Active Memory, which carries context across sessions, and Active Focus, which keeps multi-step agents from drifting between apps. Independent benchmarks from Artificial Analysis put Claude Opus 5.5 at 58 on its composite index, Muse Wonder Full tied with Sonnet 5.5 at 56, and the API-facing Muse Wonder at 52. Meta's own scorecard shows Wonder Full leading on long-horizon coding and legal-agent tasks on tests the company built itself, which is noted but not controlled against the independent index.

The release lands against a rebuilt Superintelligence Lab, a $125–145 billion 2026 capex plan, and a frontier field already crowded with Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Fable 5.1, and Gemini 4 Argon. Meta's full safety report was not published at launch — the model card acknowledges Wonder Full may reach the high-risk threshold for chemical and biological threats without mitigations, with safeguards bringing all three risk domains to "moderate or lower." On ExploitGym cyber red-teaming, 21 of 92 captured flags came through intended vulnerabilities; the other 71 came through unintended weaknesses.

A takeaway for learners: a model at Opus 5.5's price that scores two points below Opus 5.5 on an independent benchmark is a bet that persistent memory and agent reliability are the next axis of competition, not peak reasoning. Watch whether users keep paying for memory features once the novelty wears off — that is the real test of the thesis, and the signal that distinguishes a product bet from a benchmark race.
